overview.title: Learn
overview.intro: When you can’t place a digit, look for a candidate you can cross out. A few removals can leave a cell with only one choice.
difficultyParagraphs: Easy moves look for a single choice, such as the last place a digit can go in a house. Medium moves use small sets of candidates or the overlap between a line and a box. Hard patterns can span several houses. Unfair moves often need longer chains or more cases to check. For an Extreme move, you may have to follow several possible placements and see where each one leads.
The menu puts each lesson under its easiest variant. The labels below show the range for that lesson. A puzzle’s rating counts the whole solve, including how many steps it takes.

fundamentals.title: Fundamentals
fundamentals.summary: Read a cell address and work out which digits can go there.

paragraphs: Pick an empty cell with several placed digits in its row, column, or box. Cross off every digit those three houses already contain.
If one digit remains, you can place it. If several remain, try a cell whose houses contain more distinct digits.
A house is a row, a column, or a 3×3 box. Thick lines mark the boxes. Each house must contain the digits 1 through 9 once each. The digits you start with are called givens, or clues.
Every cell belongs to three houses. A line is either a row or a column.
Count rows down from the top and columns across from the left. Both counts start at 1. To find R2C4, go to row 2 and across to column 4.
Number the boxes across the top first, then across the middle, then across the bottom. The top-left box is box 1 and the bottom-right box is box 9.
Two cells that share a house see each other. They can’t hold the same digit. These cells are also called peers.
R2C4 shares row 2 with R2C5 and column 4 with R3C4. It also sees R3C5 through box 2.
The small digits in an empty cell are its candidates. To work them out, start with 1 through 9 and cross off the digits you find in the cell’s three houses.

copy.description: Check R2C4. Row 2 rules out 2, 4, and 9.
copy.reason: Column 4 rules out five more digits, 1, 5, 6, 7, and 8. You’ve already crossed off the digits you see in box 2. Only 3 is left.

paragraphs: Place the 3. A cell with just one candidate gives you a naked single. This can also happen later, after another move lets you cross out a candidate.

blocks.title: Place a single
blocks.instruction: Pick an empty cell with one candidate. Enter that digit.

groups.title: Singles
groups.overview: Three checks can give you a digit to place. Look for the last empty cell in a house, the last candidate in a cell, or the last place a digit can go in a house.

lessons.title: Full House
lessons.summary: Fill the last empty cell in a house.

paragraphs: Scan rows, columns, and boxes for a house with eight filled cells. Count which digit from 1 to 9 is missing.
If the house has two or more gaps, try a different house.
Look for a house with eight digits filled in. Check which digit from 1 to 9 is missing and put it in the gap.
For a box, count the nine cells inside its thick border. If you find two gaps in a house, check the candidates in each empty cell to see if one has a single choice.

lessons.title: Naked Single
lessons.summary: Place a digit when it’s the only candidate left in its cell.

paragraphs: Start with an empty cell that shares houses with many placed digits. Compare the digits already in its row, column, and box.
If those houses rule out eight different digits, place the one that remains. With candidates shown, look for a cell with one candidate.
Pick an empty cell. Cross off the digits you see in its three houses. One candidate left means you can fill the cell.
Check a cell again after you erase candidates. A pair, for instance, can cut a cell’s two candidates down to one.

lessons.title: Hidden Single
lessons.summary: Place a digit when it has only one possible cell in a house.

paragraphs: Pick a digit that already appears in several boxes. Find a box that still needs it and use the placed copies to rule out rows and columns.
If exactly one empty cell in the box can take the digit, place it there. You can also search one row or column at a time.
Choose a digit a house still needs. Check every empty cell in that house for it. If just one cell can take the digit, put it there. Other candidates in that cell make the single easy to miss.

items: In a row, look for copies of your digit in the crossing columns and boxes.
In a column, check the crossing rows and boxes.
In a box, follow the rows and columns through the box. A placed copy on either line rules out the cells it crosses.

groups.title: Box and line
groups.overview: Say a box can put its 5 only in row 2. Wherever the 5 goes in that box, it also fills row 2’s spot for 5. Cross out 5 from row 2 outside the box. You can also start in the row and make removals in the box.

lessons.title: Locked Candidates
lessons.summary: Erase a candidate when its only places in one house are also in another.

paragraphs: Highlight one digit and look for a box where all its candidates line up in one row or column. This is the start of pointing.
For claiming, start with a row or column whose candidates for that digit all fall in one box. Continue if the other house still has the digit as a candidate outside the overlap.
A line crosses three cells of a box. When one house has to put a digit in those three cells, both houses get the digit from that placement.

Check where a digit can go in the box. If all its candidates sit on one line, erase the digit from that line outside the box. Two candidates in the box make a pointing pair. Three make a pointing triple.
Read along a row or column. If all its candidates for your digit sit inside one box, the line has claimed that box’s copy. Erase the digit from the rest of the box.

groups.title: Pairs, triples, and quadruples
groups.overview: Two cells in a house each show only 2 and 7. Those two cells need both digits, so the rest of the house loses them. For a hidden pair, look for the 2s and 7s first. If those digits have only the same two cells available, erase the other candidates from those cells. Triples and quadruples use the same count, with more marks to keep track of.

lessons.title: Naked Subsets
lessons.summary: When several cells have just enough digits to fill them, erase those digits from the rest of the house.

paragraphs: Pick a house with several short candidate lists. Start with two cells that each have the same two candidates.
For a triple or quadruple, add cells whose candidates mostly repeat digits you have already counted. Continue when the number of distinct digits matches the number of cells.
If the cells all sit in the overlap of a line and a box, look for removals in both houses.
Pick cells in one house and count the different digits in their candidate lists. Three cells with only three digits between them have to use all three. The same count works with two or four cells.
Two cells each show only 4 and 6. Whichever takes 4, the other takes 6. Erase 4 and 6 from the rest of the house.
A triple could have cells with 2 and 3, 2 and 5, and 3 and 5. Together they need all of 2, 3, and 5. Erase those digits from the rest of the house.
The lists 12, 24, 34, and 123 contain only four distinct digits. In one house, those four cells take up 1, 2, 3, and 4. Erase the four digits elsewhere in the house.
When both cells sit where a line crosses a box, the pair uses its digits in both houses. Erase them from the other cells of the line and the box.
Three cells can also fill the stretch where a line crosses a box. Erase the triple’s digits in both houses. A quadruple is too large for that three-cell overlap.

lessons.title: Hidden Subsets
lessons.summary: If several digits have only the same few cells available, erase the other candidates from those cells.

paragraphs: In one house, pick a missing digit with only two or three possible cells. Look for other missing digits whose candidates fit inside that same small set of cells.
Continue if the number of cells equals the number of chosen digits. Look inside those cells for candidates outside the chosen digits.
Start with digits a house still needs. Count every cell that can take at least one of your chosen digits. If there are as many cells as digits, those cells are all spoken for.
When two digits can only go in the same two cells, those cells have to take the pair. Check all nine cells of the house before you erase the other candidates in those two cells.
Count the cells that can take any of three digits. If there are exactly three such cells in the house, erase their other candidates. A cell can show any one, two, or all three of the chosen digits.
Try four digits that appear only a few times each. Before you erase the other candidates from their four cells, scan the whole house for another copy of any of the chosen digits.

groups.title: Fish
groups.overview: Suppose rows 1 and 5 can put a 2 only in columns 7 and 8. Both rows need a 2, and they have to use different columns. Erase the other 2s in those columns. A Swordfish uses three lines each way and a Jellyfish uses four. With extra candidates, called fins, check what you can erase whether a fin is placed or all fins are ruled out.

lessons.title: X-Wing
lessons.summary: Look for two rows that use the same two columns for a digit, or the same pattern turned sideways.

paragraphs: Pick one digit. Find a row with exactly two places for it and scan the other rows for the same two columns.
A row with a few extra candidates in one box is worth checking for a fin. If a corner is missing, check the sashimi version. You can start with columns as well.
Look for a digit with exactly two places in each of two rows, lined up in the same columns. One row takes one column and the other takes the second. That uses up both columns for this digit.
With a pair of rows, erase the digit from both columns outside those rows. If you spot the rectangle by checking two columns first, erase from the crossing rows outside those columns.

The four corners can come with extra candidates, called fins, outside the crossing lines. All fins must share a box. A target sits in that box on a crossing line, outside the starting lines. If a fin takes the digit, the box rules out the target. If all fins are gone, the X-Wing rules it out.

Set the fins aside and look at what’s left of the rectangle. With a sashimi, one starting line has only one corner left. That corner fixes the digit in one crossing line, and the other starting line uses the second. Check for removals in the same part of the fin box.

lessons.title: Swordfish
lessons.summary: Find a digit that three rows can place only in the same three columns.

paragraphs: Pick one digit and mark the columns it can use in rows with two or three places for it. Start with two rows whose candidates mostly line up.
Look for a third row that fits the same three columns. If some candidates fall outside those columns, keep looking only if those extras share one box. You can also start with columns.

Look across three rows for one digit. Each row must have at least two candidates, and together they can use only three columns. Those rows need three copies in distinct columns. Erase the other candidates in those columns. You can also start with three columns and erase from the crossing rows.

Set aside the candidates outside the crossing lines. If they all sit in one box and you can see an ordinary Swordfish without them, check where the crossing lines enter that box. Erase only outside the starting lines. A fin in the box rules out the target if it takes the digit, and the Swordfish rules it out if all fins are gone.

If at least one starting line has just one candidate once you set the fins aside, you have a sashimi. That candidate fixes one of the three placements. The others still have to use different crossing lines. Look for the same targets as in the finned version.

lessons.title: Jellyfish
lessons.summary: Find a digit that four rows can place only in the same four columns.

paragraphs: Pick one digit and start with rows whose candidates fall in only a few columns. Add rows that reuse those columns.
Check for four rows that use four columns between them. For a finned version, all candidates outside those four columns must share a box. You can also start with columns.

Pick a digit and four rows with at least two candidates each. Count the distinct columns that contain those candidates. If the count is four, those four rows use up the columns for that digit. Erase the other copies in the columns. Four starting columns work the same way.

If you have a Jellyfish plus a few extra candidates outside the crossing lines, check where the extras are. They must all be in one box. The target is in that box and on a crossing line, outside the starting lines. It loses if a fin takes the digit and if the Jellyfish uses up the crossing lines.

When you set the fins aside, one or more starting lines can be left with just one candidate. Those candidates fix some of the placements. All four starting lines still need different crossing lines. Use the same target area as for a finned Jellyfish.

groups.title: Single-digit patterns
groups.overview: When a house has two places for a digit, crossing out one forces the other. A Skyscraper and a Two-String Kite use two such pairs. An Empty Rectangle uses one pair and the way candidates line up in a box. In each, trace the possible placements to find a candidate that loses in either case.

lessons.title: Skyscraper
lessons.summary: Find two rows with two places each for a digit and one pair of ends in the same column.

paragraphs: Pick one digit and find two rows with exactly two places each for it. Look for pairs with one column in common and different columns at the other ends.
Continue if another candidate for the digit can see both of those other ends. You can turn the same search sideways.
Pick a digit with two candidates in each of two rows. Find a candidate in one row directly above the matching candidate in the other. The two far ends must sit in different columns.

Only one of the aligned cells can take the digit. At least one row has to put it at its far end. Erase the digit from cells that see both far ends. You can also use two columns with one pair of ends in the same row.

lessons.title: Two-String Kite
lessons.summary: Join a row pair and a column pair for one digit through the box they share.

paragraphs: Find a row with exactly two places for one digit. Look for a column with exactly two places for the same digit.
Continue if one end of each pair shares a box with the other. Check whether another candidate sees both far ends.

Find a row and a column with exactly two places each for the same digit. You need four different cells, with one end from each pair in the same box. Only one of those ends can take the digit, so at least one far end has to take it.

For each kite, erase the digit from cells that see both far ends. A second pair can use the same joining cells in the box. Trace the two kites separately so you use the right far ends for each removal.

lessons.title: Empty Rectangle
lessons.summary: Use a box’s two candidate lines and a pair outside it to erase a candidate.

paragraphs: Pick one digit in a box. Look for candidates that all fit on one row and one column, with candidates on both arms.
Look outside the box for a row or column with only two places for that digit. Continue if one end lines up with an arm of the box.

Pick one digit in a box. All its candidates must fit along one row and one column, with marks on both arms. The four cells off those lines give the pattern its name. The cell where the arms meet can also show the digit.

Find a line outside the box with only two places for the digit. One end of the pair must line up with one arm. If that end takes the digit, the box has to put its copy on the other arm. Look for a target on that other arm’s line that also sees the far end of the pair. Either placement rules it out.

You can start from either arm. If the target and the far end are the only two places for the digit in their line, follow the same argument backwards for a second removal. When the box has just two candidates, you can also read the pattern as a short X-Chain.

groups.title: Almost locked sets
groups.overview: An almost locked set has one extra candidate digit. Links between these sets explain ALS-XZ, ALS-XY-Wing, ALS Chains, and many WXYZ-Wings.

lessons.title: Almost Locked Sets (ALS)
lessons.summary: One extra candidate digit lets a set connect to another set and force a removal.

paragraphs: Start with a cell that has two candidates, or two cells in one house with three distinct candidates. Look for a second set nearby that shares a digit.
Keep the connection if every copy of the shared digit in one set sees every copy in the other. Then look for another shared digit or a link to a third set.
An almost locked set (ALS) contains one more candidate digit than cells. All its cells share one house.
A cell with candidates 2 and 7 is an ALS. Two cells in one row with candidates 1, 2, and 3 between them also form an ALS.

blocks.title: One digit short of a locked subset

paragraphs: A naked pair has two cells and two candidate digits. An ALS with two cells has three candidate digits.
If one digit is absent from an ALS, its cells must use every other digit. The ALS then becomes a locked subset.
For example, two cells in one row contain {1, 2} and {2, 3}. Without 1, they must take 2 and 3.
Two separate ALSs can share a restricted common candidate, called X. Every cell that contains X in one set sees every X cell in the other.
The sets cannot both use X. At least one set must therefore use all its other digits.
If both sets contain another digit Z, at least one set must use Z. If an outside cell sees every Z candidate in both sets, it loses Z.

blocks.title: The shared digits in this example

paragraphs: The column set contains R3C7 and R5C7, with digits 1, 3, and 4. The row set contains R2C4, R2C5, R2C7, and R2C9.
The row set has five candidate digits: 1, 3, 4, 5, and 9. Both sets therefore have one more candidate digit than cells.
Their 3 candidates both lie in column 7, so the sets cannot both use 3. At least one set must use 1.
R2C8 sees every 1 candidate in both sets. It therefore loses candidate 1.

blocks.title: Named patterns in the ALS family

items: ALS-XZ connects two ALSs through a restricted common candidate.
A common WXYZ-Wing is an ALS-XZ pattern with four cells in total. The wing combines ALSs rather than forming one ALS.
ALS-XY-Wing connects three ALSs through two different restricted common candidates.
An ALS Chain connects a sequence of ALSs. Each internal set uses different digits for its incoming and outgoing links.

paragraphs: The names describe different arrangements of the same idea. A forced digit in one ALS restricts the choices in another.

lessons.title: Death Blossom
lessons.summary: Use a stem cell and its almost locked sets to rule out a digit that every stem choice forces.

paragraphs: Pick a cell with few candidates. Call it the stem. For each stem digit, find an almost locked set that contains that digit.
Check that the stem sees every copy of its linked digit in each set. Then look for a different digit that every set shares.

Each set is a petal. An almost locked set has one more distinct candidate digit than it has cells, and its cells share a house. If the stem takes a linked digit, its petal loses that digit. The petal must then use every remaining digit.
A target cell must see every copy of the shared digit in every petal. One unseen copy gives that petal a way to use the digit without ruling out the target.

copy.description: The stem R6C9 has 1, 5, and 7. The petal for 1 is R8C1, R8C2, R8C3, and R8C9. The petal for 5 is R4C4 and R6C6. The petal for 7 is R4C4 and R6C4. All three petals contain 3.
copy.reason: Whatever goes in R6C9, its petal loses that digit and must use 3. R8C4 sees every possible 3 in all three petals, so you can remove its 3.

guide.start: Pick a cell with few candidates. Call it the stem. For each stem digit, find an almost locked set that contains that digit.
guide.check: Check that the stem sees every copy of its linked digit in each set. Then look for a different digit that every set shares.
guide.reason: One stem digit must be true. That choice forces the shared digit into its petal. A candidate that sees every possible placement across the petals can go.

lessons.title: Sue de Coq
lessons.summary: Split the candidates in a box and line intersection into two groups that lock digits into their houses.

paragraphs: Find two or three empty cells where a box and a line overlap. Look for extra digits beyond the number of cells in that intersection.
Find a set in the rest of the line and a set in the rest of the box. Check that their digit groups are disjoint.

copy.description: The diagram highlights the shared cells and both side sets. Read each crossed-out candidate against the set in its own house.
copy.reason: The side sets use up the extra choices. The intersection and the line set lock their group into the line. The intersection and the box set do the same in the box.

guide.start: Find two or three empty cells where a box and a line overlap. Look for extra digits beyond the number of cells in that intersection.
guide.check: Find a set in the rest of the line and a set in the rest of the box. Check that their digit groups are disjoint.
guide.reason: The side sets use up the extra choices. The intersection and the line set lock their group into the line. The intersection and the box set do the same in the box.

groups.title: Wings
groups.overview: In an XY-Wing, either choice for the middle cell makes one of the two wings take the same digit. A cell that sees both wings loses that candidate. The other wings use different ways to force a digit. With WXYZ-Wing, check which digits could occur twice in the four cells.

lessons.title: XY-Wing
lessons.summary: Either digit in the pivot makes one of the wings take their common digit.

paragraphs: Pick a cell with two candidates. For each of those digits, look for a cell it sees with exactly two candidates, one of which is that digit.
Continue if the two outside cells share the same extra digit. Look for another cell with that digit that sees both outside cells.
In the example, the middle cell, or pivot, has 1 and 2. Look for two cells that see it. One has only 1 and 3 and the other has only 2 and 3. Those two cells are the wings.

A 1 in the pivot leaves the 1 and 3 wing with 3. A 2 leaves the other wing with 3. Erase 3 anywhere that sees both wings. Check each wing against the pivot separately. They can see it through different houses.

lessons.title: XYZ-Wing
lessons.summary: The pivot holds the wings’ common digit, so a target has to see all three cells.

paragraphs: Pick a cell with three candidates. Look for two cells it sees that each contain only two of those three digits.
Continue if the pairs share one digit and together cover all three. A target must have that shared digit and see all three cells.
The pivot in the figure has 2, 8, and 9. The wings see the pivot and have only 2 and 8, or 8 and 9. If the pivot takes 2 or 9, one wing takes 8. The pivot could also take 8 itself.
Erase 8 from a cell that sees all three. R6C5 sees the wing in R2C5 through column 5, and sees the pivot and the other wing through the middle box.

lessons.title: W-Wing
lessons.summary: Link two cells with the same two candidates so one wing must take the other digit.

paragraphs: Find two cells that have the same two candidates. Pick one of those digits and look for a house with exactly two places for it.
Keep looking if each end of that pair sees a different starting cell. A target for the other digit must see both starting cells.
In the figure, both wings have 5 and 7. Column 2 has just two places for 7, and each of those places sees a different wing. Whichever place takes 7 leaves the wing it sees with only 5.
Erase 5 in any cell that sees both wings. If you find a house with two places for 5 instead, use that link to look for a removal of 7.

lessons.title: WXYZ-Wing
lessons.summary: Four cells with four digits can force a digit across houses.

paragraphs: Start with a cell that has a short candidate list. Add nearby cells that reuse those digits until four cells contain exactly four distinct digits between them.
For each digit, check whether all its copies in the four cells see one another. Keep the pattern if at least three digits pass this check.

Pick four cells with exactly four different candidates between them. Look at one digit at a time. If all the cells that could take it in the wing see one another, that digit is restricted. Only one of those cells can take it.
An almost locked set (ALS) has one more candidate digit than cells. All its cells share one house.
A common WXYZ-Wing connects two ALSs with four cells in total. This arrangement is a small ALS-XZ pattern.
The whole wing can span several houses. It is not necessarily one ALS.
If three digits are restricted, they can fill at most three cells. The fourth digit has to fill at least one. Erase it from a cell that sees every place it could go in the wing.
R4C3, R4C4, and R4C6 form a three-cell ALS with digits 1, 2, 5, and 9. R6C1 forms another ALS with candidates 1 and 9.
The two 1 candidates share box 4, so the sets cannot both use 1. At least one set must use 9.
R4C2 sees all the 9 candidates in both sets. It therefore loses candidate 9.
The restricted-digit count also explains this removal. It does not require every four-cell arrangement to have the same ALS layout.

All four cells need digits, so when every digit is restricted, each goes in exactly one cell. For each digit, erase it from cells that see all its places in the wing. With two unrestricted digits, this count gives no specific digit to erase.

references.label: Almost Locked Sets (ALS): the shared idea

groups.title: Coloring and chains
groups.overview: Use two colors to mark candidates that would be placed together. If one color puts the same digit in a house twice, the other color wins. In a chain, follow one candidate at a time to see what placing or removing it forces. Some chains switch digits, use groups of candidates, or join their ends to form a loop.

lessons.title: Simple Coloring
lessons.summary: Use two colors to follow the possible placements of one digit.

paragraphs: Pick one digit and find a row, column, or box with exactly two places for it. Color the candidates differently.
At each end, look for another house where that digit also has exactly two places. Keep going while you can add links, then check for a conflict within one color or a candidate that sees both.

Find two candidates for the same digit that are the only places for it in one house. Color them differently. When either candidate forms another such pair, color the new end with the opposite color. Within one connected set, placing one color rules out the other.
If an uncolored candidate sees one of each color, it can’t take the digit whichever color is placed. Erase it.

Two candidates of the same color can’t both be placed if they see each other. Erase that color throughout the connected set and place the other color. Give disconnected sets their own colors until you can link them.
Check whether every candidate for the digit in a house would disappear if you placed one color. That would leave the house without the digit. Erase that color and place the other one.

lessons.title: 3D Medusa
lessons.summary: Use cells with two candidates to carry two-color reasoning from one digit to another.

paragraphs: Start at a cell with exactly two candidates and give them opposite colors. Pick either digit and look for a house where it has exactly one other spot.
Give that other spot the opposite color. If it is in a cell with two candidates, switch digits there and look for another link. Follow each connected branch.
If a link stops, check the other branches. Look for a conflict within one color or a candidate that either color would rule out.

Color the two places for a digit as in Simple Coloring. When you reach a cell with exactly two candidates, its other mark gets the opposite color. Keep following pairs in houses and in cells. In the connected set, all the candidates of one color can be placed together when that color is true.

blocks.title: When one color breaks a rule

items: One cell would get two digits of the same color.
One house would get two copies of the same digit.
Placing the color would erase every candidate from an empty cell.
Placing the color would leave a house with no place for a missing digit.

paragraphs: Any one of these checks rules out the entire color. Place the candidates of the other color in this set.

blocks.title: When either color rules out the same candidate

items: A cell contains both colors. Both choices for the cell rule out its uncolored candidates.
An uncolored candidate sees its own digit in both colors. It loses whichever color is placed.
An uncolored candidate has one color in its cell and sees its own digit in the other color. Either placement rules it out.

lessons.title: X-Chain
lessons.summary: Follow strong and weak links for one digit to find a candidate that sees both ends.

paragraphs: Pick a digit with exactly two places in a house. From one end, find another candidate for that digit that it sees.
Keep the new candidate if it has a house with a second two-place link. After a strong link, look for an outside candidate that sees both ends.

When a house has just two places for a digit, the pair forms a strong link. If one end is ruled out, the other must be placed. Any two candidates for the same digit that see each other form a weak link. If one end is placed, the other must be ruled out.

Use a strong link at each end of the chain and alternate the links in between. Rule out the first candidate and trace the result. At each solid link, place the next candidate. At each dashed link, rule it out. This forces the final candidate, so a cell that sees both ends loses the digit.
A Skyscraper or Two-String Kite uses three links. You can keep going through more houses as long as the links alternate and the last one is strong.

lessons.title: XY-Chain
lessons.summary: Link cells with two candidates until the same digit appears at both ends.

paragraphs: Start at a cell with two candidates. Pick one digit as the starting end. Use the other digit to find a cell you can see with exactly two candidates that includes it.
Switch to the other digit in each new cell. Continue until a far end has the starting digit and another candidate for that digit sees both ends.

Pick one candidate to cross out in a cell with two marks. That forces its other digit. Find another two-candidate cell that sees the first and shares the forced digit. Cross out that digit there and use the other mark to continue.

Stop when the last cell has to take the digit you first crossed out. One of the two ends has to take it. Erase that digit wherever a cell sees both ends. An XY-Wing uses the same argument with three cells.

lessons.title: Alternating Inference Chains
lessons.summary: Follow alternating links to show that at least one end of the chain must be true.

paragraphs: Start with a strong link. Look for a cell with two candidates or a digit with exactly two places in a house.
From the far end, find a candidate that conflicts with it and has a strong link of its own. Keep alternating. After a strong link, look for a candidate that conflicts with both ends.
For a grouped chain, also look for several spots for one digit in the same stretch of a box and a line. Treat the group as one end.

Use a strong link at both ends and alternate strong and weak links in between. Suppose the first candidate is false. A strong link forces the next candidate to be true, then a weak link makes the next one false. Continue to the last link, which forces the candidate at that end.

blocks.title: Type 1 with the same digit at both ends

paragraphs: If the ends show the same digit, erase it from any cell that sees both. The links in the middle can switch digits.

Suppose the ends are 2 in cell A and 7 in cell B, and the two cells see each other. A 7 in A would cross out the 2 in A and the 7 in B, leaving both ends false. Erase 7 from A. The same reasoning rules out 2 in B if it’s there.

Candidates for one digit where a line crosses a box can act as a single end of a link. The group is true when any member is true. A weak link into the group has to rule out all its members. A strong link can join two groups, or a group and a single candidate, if they cover every place for the digit in a house.

lessons.title: Nice Loops
lessons.summary: Follow a chain back to the same candidate and check the two links that meet there.

paragraphs: Start at a candidate with several links, such as a digit in a cell with two candidates and a two-place link in its row.
Alternate strong and weak links. Continue if a link can return to the original candidate or group. Check whether the first and last links match.
Start at a candidate and alternate strong and weak links until you’re back where you started. The first and last links can be different or the same. The deduction comes from that join.

With two weak links at the join, assume the starting candidate is true. The loop takes you back to that candidate and makes it false, so erase it. With two strong links, starting with it false forces it to be true. Place it.

If the links alternate at the join, pick a weak link and assume one end is false. Follow the rest of the loop to force the other end true. Any candidate that conflicts with both ends can go. Check each weak link separately.
A group stands for at least one of its candidates. When a link makes the group false, all its candidates are false. Trace the rest of the loop to see whether it contradicts the starting assumption.

At least one end of the weak link must be true. When one end is a group, the target has to conflict with every member of that group and with the other end. If both ends are groups, check all the members at both ends.

lessons.title: ALS alternating inference chain
lessons.summary: Use an almost locked set as a strong link in an alternating inference chain.

paragraphs: Find an almost locked set with two useful digit groups. If the set skips the first digit, it must use the second digit.
Connect the groups to outside candidates that see every copy of the relevant digit in the set. Keep alternating strong and weak links.

copy.description: Trace the chain through the ALS. Each group in the set stands for all the candidate cells for its digit.
copy.reason: The ALS supplies an at-least-one link. After you build a chain with strong end links, at least one end is true. A candidate that conflicts with both ends can go.

guide.start: Find an almost locked set with two useful digit groups. If the set skips the first digit, it must use the second digit.
guide.check: Connect the groups to outside candidates that see every copy of the relevant digit in the set. Keep alternating strong and weak links.
guide.reason: The ALS supplies an at-least-one link. After you build a chain with strong end links, at least one end is true. A candidate that conflicts with both ends can go.

lessons.title: ALS discontinuous Nice Loop
lessons.summary: Use an ALS link in a loop that forces one candidate at the break in alternation.

paragraphs: Find an ALS that links two groups of candidates. Trace an alternating path that goes through the set and comes back to its starting candidate.
Compare the strengths of the two links that touch the starting candidate. Two weak links force a removal. Two strong links force a placement.

copy.description: Follow the proof across the ALS and back to the candidate where the two links have the same strength.
copy.reason: If both meeting links are weak, placing the starting candidate eventually rules it out. If both are strong, ruling it out eventually forces it.

guide.start: Find an ALS that links two groups of candidates. Trace an alternating path that goes through the set and comes back to its starting candidate.
guide.check: Compare the strengths of the two links that touch the starting candidate. Two weak links force a removal. Two strong links force a placement.
guide.reason: If both meeting links are weak, placing the starting candidate eventually rules it out. If both are strong, ruling it out eventually forces it.

lessons.title: ALS continuous Nice Loop
lessons.summary: Close an alternating loop through an ALS and use the weak links to remove candidates.

paragraphs: Start with a strong link supplied by an almost locked set. Trace alternating weak and strong links until the path returns to its first node.
Check that the first and last links have different strengths. On a weak link, find outside candidates that conflict with both ends.

copy.description: The closed chain alternates at every junction. Match each removal to the weak link whose ends it conflicts with.
copy.reason: Every weak link in a continuous loop gains an at-least-one guarantee. An outside candidate that conflicts with both ends would break that guarantee.

guide.start: Start with a strong link supplied by an almost locked set. Trace alternating weak and strong links until the path returns to its first node.
guide.check: Check that the first and last links have different strengths. On a weak link, find outside candidates that conflict with both ends.
guide.reason: Every weak link in a continuous loop gains an at-least-one guarantee. An outside candidate that conflicts with both ends would break that guarantee.

groups.title: Uniqueness
groups.overview: On a puzzle with one solution, any arrangement that lets you swap digits and keep a valid grid can be ruled out. A Unique Rectangle looks for a swap across four corners. BUG+1 looks for a swap across all the empty cells.

lessons.title: Unique Rectangle
lessons.summary: Look for four corners where swapping two digits would give a second solution.

paragraphs: On a puzzle with one solution, start at a cell with only two candidates. Look for that same pair in a second cell in its row or column.
Look across those lines for two more cells that both contain the pair. Continue if the four corners span exactly two boxes. The extra candidates and strong links tell you which version to use.

Use this on a puzzle with exactly one solution. Look for four empty corners in two rows and two columns, across exactly two boxes. All four can take the same two digits. If they used only those digits, each diagonal would hold one of them. You could swap the two digits without changing which digits any house contains. At least one corner has to use an extra digit to prevent that swap.

blocks.title: Type 1 with extras in one corner

paragraphs: If three corners have only the pair, the fourth has to use an extra digit. Erase both digits of the pair from that corner.

blocks.title: Type 2 with the same extra on adjacent corners

paragraphs: Look for two neighboring corners with the same extra digit and the other two corners with just the pair. One of the two extras must be placed. Erase that digit in any cell that sees both corners with the extra.

blocks.title: Type 3 with a subset of extra digits

paragraphs: Two adjacent corners have extras, and between them they need at least one extra digit. Count the two corners as one slot for those digits. Add cells from a house they share until the number of distinct digits equals the number of slots. Erase those digits from the other cells of that house.

blocks.title: Type 4 with a strong link on one side

paragraphs: Two adjacent corners have extras. Look for a digit of the rectangle pair that has only those two places in a shared house. One corner must take it. If the other corner took the second digit of the pair, all four corners would use only the pair. Erase the second digit from both corners with extras.

blocks.title: Type 5 with the same extra across the diagonals

paragraphs: Find the same extra digit in two opposite corners or in three corners, with no other extras. At least one of those corners must take the extra. Erase it from any cell that sees all the corners where it appears.

blocks.title: Type 6 with one digit locked to a diagonal

paragraphs: The two corners with extras are opposite each other. Find a digit of the pair whose only places in both rows and both columns are the four corners. It must take one whole diagonal. If it took the diagonal with extras, the other two corners would take the second digit and allow the swap. Erase the linked digit from the corners with extras.

Start at a corner that contains just the pair and look at the opposite corner. One digit of the pair must have no places beyond the rectangle in that opposite corner’s row and column. If the opposite corner took the other digit, both lines would force the rectangle into the swappable arrangement. Erase that other digit from the opposite corner.

The swap can also involve digits you’ve already placed. Check that none of the corners is a given. With three filled corners, erase the candidate that would complete the swap. With two filled corners and the same extra candidate in both empty corners, erase that extra from cells that see both empty corners.

The swap has to respect the givens. A rectangle digit might have been crossed out during an earlier move even though the givens allow it there. Check that both digits could go in all four corners from the givens before you use this version.

lessons.title: BUG+1
lessons.summary: In a puzzle with one solution, look for the extra candidate that keeps all the empty cells from having two choices.

paragraphs: Scan the empty cells for short candidate lists. Keep looking if exactly one cell has three candidates and every other empty cell has two.
In the row, column, and box of the three-candidate cell, count the possible spots for each of its digits. Look for the digit that has three spots in all three houses.

BUG stands for Bivalue Universal Grave. In a BUG, every empty cell has two candidates and every missing digit has two places in each house that needs it. If you solved that grid, changing every originally empty cell to its other digit would still leave one of each digit in every house. You’d have two solutions.

For BUG+1, look for one cell with three candidates and two candidates in every other empty cell. In the three-candidate cell, find the digit with three places in each of its houses. If crossing it out leaves a BUG, solving without that candidate would let you swap the choices to make another solution. A one-solution puzzle has to use the extra digit.
Check the counts across the grid before placing it. A cell with three candidates can also occur without a BUG pattern.

lessons.title: Unique Loop
lessons.summary: Extend the two-digit uniqueness argument from a rectangle to a longer ring.

paragraphs: In a puzzle with one solution, follow two shared digits along a ring of cells. Each affected row, column, and box must meet the ring in a pair.
Follow the alternating placements around the ring. Check that you can swap the two digits and still satisfy the same houses.

copy.description: In this example, one loop cell supplies the extra choice. Remove the two shared digits from that cell.
copy.reason: If every loop cell used just the two shared digits, a swap would give another solution. An extra candidate must break the swap.

guide.start: In a puzzle with one solution, follow two shared digits along a ring of cells. Each affected row, column, and box must meet the ring in a pair.
guide.check: Follow the alternating placements around the ring. Check that you can swap the two digits and still satisfy the same houses.
guide.reason: If every loop cell used just the two shared digits, a swap would give another solution. An extra candidate must break the swap.

lessons.title: Unique Rectangle alternating inference chain
lessons.summary: Use the extra candidates of a Unique Rectangle as a strong link in an open chain.

paragraphs: In a puzzle with one solution, find a rectangle that spans two boxes and shares a pair of digits in all four corners.
Collect the extra candidates that can break the swap. The two ends of the rectangle link must cover every such choice.

copy.description: Find the rectangle link within the chain. The link connects the choices that keep the two digits from swapping.
copy.reason: At least one extra candidate must be true, so the rectangle can supply a strong link. Follow the full chain and remove a candidate that conflicts with both ends.

guide.start: In a puzzle with one solution, find a rectangle that spans two boxes and shares a pair of digits in all four corners.
guide.check: Collect the extra candidates that can break the swap. The two ends of the rectangle link must cover every such choice.
guide.reason: At least one extra candidate must be true, so the rectangle can supply a strong link. Follow the full chain and remove a candidate that conflicts with both ends.

lessons.title: Unique Rectangle discontinuous Nice Loop
lessons.summary: Use a rectangle’s extra candidates to close a loop with a break in alternation.

paragraphs: Start with a Unique Rectangle and group its extras into two choices. Use the at-least-one link between those groups in an alternating path.
Close the path at a single candidate. Check whether both links there are weak or both are strong.

copy.description: Trace the loop to the two strong links at its break. The highlighted placement follows from those links.
copy.reason: The two weak links make the candidate false. The two strong links make it true. The rectangle link relies on the puzzle having one solution.

guide.start: Start with a Unique Rectangle and group its extras into two choices. Use the at-least-one link between those groups in an alternating path.
guide.check: Close the path at a single candidate. Check whether both links there are weak or both are strong.
guide.reason: The two weak links make the candidate false. The two strong links make it true. The rectangle link relies on the puzzle having one solution.

lessons.title: Unique Rectangle continuous Nice Loop
lessons.summary: Use a rectangle link in a fully alternating loop to make removals along its weak links.

paragraphs: Find a rectangle whose extra candidates give an at-least-one link. Close an alternating path that crosses this link.
Check the strengths where the last link meets the first. If the loop still alternates there, inspect each weak link for a shared conflict.

copy.description: Track which weak link supports each removal. The rectangle is one link in the loop.
copy.reason: The loop makes each weak link strong as well. At least one end of each weak link must be true, so a candidate that conflicts with both ends can go.

guide.start: Find a rectangle whose extra candidates give an at-least-one link. Close an alternating path that crosses this link.
guide.check: Check the strengths where the last link meets the first. If the loop still alternates there, inspect each weak link for a shared conflict.
guide.reason: The loop makes each weak link strong as well. At least one end of each weak link must be true, so a candidate that conflicts with both ends can go.

groups.title: Forcing proofs
groups.overview: Try a candidate and follow the moves it would force. If a house runs out of places for a digit, the original choice has to go. If every possible choice leads to the same move, make that move. A net can use several earlier deductions to force a single step.

lessons.title: Forcing Chains and Nets
lessons.summary: Follow a possible move until it breaks a rule or leads to the same result as every other choice.

paragraphs: Start at a cell with two candidates or a digit with only two places in a house. A candidate that affects several short candidate lists is also worth a try.

Try a choice and look for a single that follows from it. Keep going while changes force new moves. Look for a rule that breaks or a move that all starting choices share. For a net, record which earlier changes work together to force the next move.

Pick a candidate. Try placing it or crossing it out and track the moves that follow. A placement rules out the other digits in that cell and the same digit in its peers. Whenever a cell or a missing digit in a house has one choice left, follow that placement too.

Stop if a cell loses every candidate, a house runs out of places for a digit, or a candidate has to be both true and false. The starting assumption can’t hold. Erase a candidate if placing it caused the contradiction. Place it if crossing it out caused the contradiction.

blocks.title: All choices lead to the same move

paragraphs: Try each candidate in a cell, each place for one digit in a house, or both possibilities for a single candidate. Follow every choice separately. If they all give the same placement or removal, make that move.

A chain goes from one deduction to the next. A net can use several earlier deductions for a single step. For instance, three separate removals might leave only one place for a digit in a column. Check that each of those removals follows from the same starting assumption before you place the digit.

lessons.title: Tridagon forcing net
lessons.summary: Track the consequences of the guardians that can break a Tridagon.

paragraphs: Find a Tridagon whose extra candidates do not give a direct move. Mark each extra candidate so you have the full list of guardians.
Follow the forced changes from each guardian. Look for the same result in every case, or test a candidate that would leave no viable guardian.

copy.description: Use the guardians as starting points. The nets carry the proof past the highlighted twelve-cell pattern.
copy.reason: At least one guardian must be true. If all possible guardian branches rule out the same candidate, you can cross it out.

guide.start: Find a Tridagon whose extra candidates do not give a direct move. Mark each extra candidate so you have the full list of guardians.
guide.check: Follow the forced changes from each guardian. Look for the same result in every case, or test a candidate that would leave no viable guardian.
guide.reason: At least one guardian must be true. If all possible guardian branches rule out the same candidate, you can cross it out.

lessons.title: Dynamic forcing net
lessons.summary: Find new links as the candidates change inside a forcing branch.

paragraphs: Choose a candidate whose placement changes several nearby cells. Mark each removal it forces before continuing.
After each change, count the remaining candidates in the affected cells and houses. A new two-choice link can appear during the branch.

copy.description: Follow the forced changes in order. A later inference can depend on an earlier removal that created a link.
copy.reason: A link created inside a branch applies only in that branch. Use it to reach a contradiction or show a result shared by every starting choice.

guide.start: Choose a candidate whose placement changes several nearby cells. Mark each removal it forces before continuing.
guide.check: After each change, count the remaining candidates in the affected cells and houses. A new two-choice link can appear during the branch.
guide.reason: A link created inside a branch applies only in that branch. Use it to reach a contradiction or show a result shared by every starting choice.

references.label: HoDoKu on forcing proofs and Kraken Fish

lessons.title: Advanced forcing net
lessons.summary: Use patterns such as subsets or fish inside a forcing branch.

paragraphs: Pick a starting choice with several direct consequences. Update the candidates inside that branch as each consequence follows.
If singles and links stop, look for a supported pattern in the reduced grid. Check every premise of that pattern in the current branch.

copy.description: The diagram marks candidates used in the forcing proof. Check the intermediate pattern before using its consequences.
copy.reason: A valid pattern adds another forced step under the starting choice. A contradiction rules out that choice. The same result in every complete branch proves the move.

guide.start: Pick a starting choice with several direct consequences. Update the candidates inside that branch as each consequence follows.
guide.check: If singles and links stop, look for a supported pattern in the reduced grid. Check every premise of that pattern in the current branch.
guide.reason: A valid pattern adds another forced step under the starting choice. A contradiction rules out that choice. The same result in every complete branch proves the move.

lessons.title: Nested forcing net
lessons.summary: Open a second set of cases inside a forcing branch to establish a step.

paragraphs: Trace an outer branch until direct deductions stop. In that branch, find a cell or house with a short list of remaining choices.
Follow each inner choice separately. Carry a step back to the outer branch only when the inner proof establishes it there.

copy.description: Keep the two levels of choices separate. Trace the inner cases before accepting the next step of the outer net.
copy.reason: A move proved inside the inner cases belongs to the outer branch. Use it to finish the outer proof before drawing a conclusion about the original grid.

guide.start: Trace an outer branch until direct deductions stop. In that branch, find a cell or house with a short list of remaining choices.
guide.check: Follow each inner choice separately. Carry a step back to the outer branch only when the inner proof establishes it there.
guide.reason: A move proved inside the inner cases belongs to the outer branch. Use it to finish the outer proof before drawing a conclusion about the original grid.

groups.title: Fireworks
groups.overview: Follow digits that share the same options at a row and column crossing.

lessons.title: Fireworks
lessons.summary: Use a box pivot and two outside wings to place three or four digits into a small set of cells.

paragraphs: Pick an empty intersection of a row and column. Look for a digit with spots on both arms inside the box.
Follow both arms outside the box. For each chosen digit, check that the pivot and two wing cells cover the remaining options on those arms.

copy.description: R1C9 is the pivot. The Firework for 1, 2, and 3 uses R1C1 and R9C9 as wings.
copy.reason: A Firework digit must occupy the pivot or one of its wings. The highlighted cells supply exactly enough places for these digits, so their extra candidates can go.

guide.start: Pick an empty intersection of a row and column. Look for a digit with spots on both arms inside the box.
guide.check: Follow both arms outside the box. For each chosen digit, check that the pivot and two wing cells cover the remaining options on those arms.
guide.reason: A Firework digit must occupy the pivot or one of its wings. The highlighted cells supply exactly enough places for these digits, so their extra candidates can go.

lessons.title: Firework W-wing
lessons.summary: Use matching bivalue cells to turn a Firework pair into a removal.

paragraphs: Find two digits that share the same Firework pivot. Look for two outside cells that each contain only those two digits.
Check that each bivalue cell covers one outside arm for the other digit. The same target must also see every wing copy of its own digit.

copy.description: The crossed-out candidate sees the two possible places forced by the connected bivalue cells.
copy.reason: If the target were true, both bivalue cells would take the other digit. Both Firework digits would lose their wing copies and need the same pivot.

guide.start: Find two digits that share the same Firework pivot. Look for two outside cells that each contain only those two digits.
guide.check: Check that each bivalue cell covers one outside arm for the other digit. The same target must also see every wing copy of its own digit.
guide.reason: If the target were true, both bivalue cells would take the other digit. Both Firework digits would lose their wing copies and need the same pivot.

lessons.title: Firework L-wing
lessons.summary: Use a two-place link for a third digit to rule it out of the opposite Firework wing.

paragraphs: Find a Firework pair with one wing cell on each arm. Then look for a strong link for a third digit with one end at a wing.
Check that the other end of the strong link sees the opposite Firework wing. Test whether that wing could take the third digit.

copy.description: Follow the third digit between the two-place link and the other Firework wing.
copy.reason: The candidate would rule out the far end of the strong link. That forces the same digit into the other wing and leaves both Firework digits needing the pivot.

guide.start: Find a Firework pair with one wing cell on each arm. Then look for a strong link for a third digit with one end at a wing.
guide.check: Check that the other end of the strong link sees the opposite Firework wing. Test whether that wing could take the third digit.
guide.reason: The candidate would rule out the far end of the strong link. That forces the same digit into the other wing and leaves both Firework digits needing the pivot.

lessons.title: Firework ALS-wing
lessons.summary: Connect two Firework pairs through a shared bivalue cell.

paragraphs: Look for two Fireworks with the same digit pair. Find a cell with just those two candidates that sees every outside wing copy for both patterns.
Each choice in that cell can force the same digit into both pivots. Find where the other digit can still go in each set of wings.

copy.description: Compare the connected arms and the two pivots. The shared bivalue cell ties both Fireworks to the same choice.
copy.reason: The anchor digit must go in both pivots. The other digit must have room in both sets of wings. Check both anchor choices before removing a candidate.

guide.start: Look for two Fireworks with the same digit pair. Find a cell with just those two candidates that sees every outside wing copy for both patterns.
guide.check: Each choice in that cell can force the same digit into both pivots. Find where the other digit can still go in each set of wings.
guide.reason: The anchor digit must go in both pivots. The other digit must have room in both sets of wings. Check both anchor choices before removing a candidate.

lessons.title: Firework alternating inference chain
lessons.summary: Use the candidate choices around a Firework as a link in an alternating inference chain.

paragraphs: Look for a Firework pivot and two wings. Find two groups of candidates such that at least one group must provide the required Firework digit.
Use that at-least-one guarantee as a strong link. Look for ordinary weak links that can connect the groups to the rest of a chain.

copy.description: Trace the chain to the Firework link. Follow every candidate in a grouped end before moving to the next link.
copy.reason: A valid alternating chain with strong end links forces at least one end true. A candidate that conflicts with both ends is ruled out.

guide.start: Look for a Firework pivot and two wings. Find two groups of candidates such that at least one group must provide the required Firework digit.
guide.check: Use that at-least-one guarantee as a strong link. Look for ordinary weak links that can connect the groups to the rest of a chain.
guide.reason: A valid alternating chain with strong end links forces at least one end true. A candidate that conflicts with both ends is ruled out.

groups.title: Advanced patterns
groups.overview: Count candidate slots, test local assignments, and look for cells that break a pattern.

lessons.title: Aligned Pair Exclusion
lessons.summary: Rule out a candidate when every assignment to a pair of cells that uses it fails.

paragraphs: Choose two cells that see the same constrained neighbors. Pick a candidate in one of the two cells and list the possible digits in the other.
For each assignment that uses the chosen candidate, check for a repeated digit or a nearby cell that loses all of its candidates.

copy.description: The highlighted cells form the pair. Hold 5 fixed in R1C4 and check the other cell’s possible digits.
copy.reason: If every assignment using the chosen candidate fails, that candidate cannot be the solution. A single surviving assignment keeps it in play.

guide.start: Choose two cells that see the same constrained neighbors. Pick a candidate in one of the two cells and list the possible digits in the other.
guide.check: For each assignment that uses the chosen candidate, check for a repeated digit or a nearby cell that loses all of its candidates.
guide.reason: If every assignment using the chosen candidate fails, that candidate cannot be the solution. A single surviving assignment keeps it in play.

lessons.title: Aligned Triplet Exclusion
lessons.summary: Check three cells together to find combinations that two cells alone cannot rule out.

paragraphs: Choose three cells whose placements can affect the same constrained neighbors. Fix a candidate in one cell and list the choices in the other two.
Test each combination for a repeated digit in a house or a nearby cell left with no candidates.

copy.description: Keep 4 in R1C4 while you check the other two highlighted cells. Each assignment fails a local Sudoku rule.
copy.reason: If all combinations that contain the candidate fail, remove it. Test assignments for the other candidates separately.

guide.start: Choose three cells whose placements can affect the same constrained neighbors. Fix a candidate in one cell and list the choices in the other two.
guide.check: Test each combination for a repeated digit in a house or a nearby cell left with no candidates.
guide.reason: If all combinations that contain the candidate fail, remove it. Test assignments for the other candidates separately.

lessons.title: Tridagon
lessons.summary: Find an arrangement of three digits that needs a candidate outside the pattern.

paragraphs: Pick four boxes that form a rectangle across two bands and two stacks. In each box, choose three cells in different rows and columns.
Find three core digits. Each selected cell must allow at least two of them, and the three cells in each box must cover all three.

copy.description: The highlighted boxes contain one guardian in this example. The other cells cannot fill the pattern with just the three core digits.
copy.reason: The three core digits alone cannot fill this twelve-cell arrangement. At least one extra candidate, called a guardian, must be true.

guide.start: Pick four boxes that form a rectangle across two bands and two stacks. In each box, choose three cells in different rows and columns.
guide.check: Find three core digits. Each selected cell must allow at least two of them, and the three cells in each box must cover all three.
guide.reason: The three core digits alone cannot fill this twelve-cell arrangement. At least one extra candidate, called a guardian, must be true.

lessons.title: Tridagon alternating inference chain
lessons.summary: Turn the guardians that break a Tridagon into a strong link.

paragraphs: Find a Tridagon with multiple guardian candidates. Try dividing the guardians into two groups that together cover all the extra candidates.
Find weak links to the groups. To rule out a group, a candidate must conflict with every guardian in it.

copy.description: Locate the link between the Tridagon guardians and follow the other links to the crossed-out candidate.
copy.reason: At least one guardian must be true, so the two groups form a strong link. An alternating chain can carry that guarantee to a candidate outside the pattern.

guide.start: Find a Tridagon with multiple guardian candidates. Try dividing the guardians into two groups that together cover all the extra candidates.
guide.check: Find weak links to the groups. To rule out a group, a candidate must conflict with every guardian in it.
guide.reason: At least one guardian must be true, so the two groups form a strong link. An alternating chain can carry that guarantee to a candidate outside the pattern.

lessons.title: SK loop
lessons.summary: Count the digit slots in a ring around four placed digits.

paragraphs: Look for four givens at rectangle corners. Check the arms beside those corners for pairs of cells with shared small digit groups.
Follow the ring one house at a time. Count one slot for each linked digit in a house. The number of slots must match the number of cells in the ring.

copy.description: Follow the highlighted ring and count the slots along each arm. Use the whole ring before crossing out a candidate.
copy.reason: Each cell needs a slot and each slot can hold just one digit. An outside candidate that uses a slot, or an inside candidate that uses two, leaves too few slots.

guide.start: Look for four givens at rectangle corners. Check the arms beside those corners for pairs of cells with shared small digit groups.
guide.check: Follow the ring one house at a time. Count one slot for each linked digit in a house. The number of slots must match the number of cells in the ring.
guide.reason: Each cell needs a slot and each slot can hold just one digit. An outside candidate that uses a slot, or an inside candidate that uses two, leaves too few slots.

lessons.title: Multi-sector locked sets
lessons.summary: Lock a group of cells into an equal number of digit slots across several houses.

paragraphs: Find a group of cells whose candidates fit into a small collection of house-and-digit slots. Include nearby cells that use only those same slots.
Count the cells and the slots. Check every candidate in the set against at least one slot, and make sure each slot can hold only one placement.

copy.description: The highlighted cells include the main set and its attached cells. Count the attachments before comparing the totals.
copy.reason: If the two counts match, every slot must serve the selected cells. You can remove outside candidates using a slot and inside candidates using more than one slot.

guide.start: Find a group of cells whose candidates fit into a small collection of house-and-digit slots. Include nearby cells that use only those same slots.
guide.check: Count the cells and the slots. Check every candidate in the set against at least one slot, and make sure each slot can hold only one placement.
guide.reason: If the two counts match, every slot must serve the selected cells. You can remove outside candidates using a slot and inside candidates using more than one slot.

groups.title: Exocets
groups.overview: Track which digits must travel from a pair of base cells to targets in other boxes.

lessons.title: Junior Exocet
lessons.summary: Use three cross-lines to force digits from a base pair into target cells.

paragraphs: Look for two base cells on one line within the same box. Find target cells in the other boxes of that band or stack.
For every base digit, count the houses that cover its remaining spots on the cross-lines outside the targets. Check whether those spots can satisfy all three lines alone.

copy.description: Compare the highlighted bases with the target cells. Cross out target digits excluded by every compatible cross-line assignment.
copy.reason: A digit placed in the base pair needs a place on every cross-line. If the outside spots only cover two copies, a target must take the remaining copy.

guide.start: Look for two base cells on one line within the same box. Find target cells in the other boxes of that band or stack.
guide.check: For every base digit, count the houses that cover its remaining spots on the cross-lines outside the targets. Check whether those spots can satisfy all three lines alone.
guide.reason: A digit placed in the base pair needs a place on every cross-line. If the outside spots only cover two copies, a target must take the remaining copy.

lessons.title: Senior Exocet
lessons.summary: Use cross-line cover counts with a target beyond the Junior Exocet arrangement.

paragraphs: Start with a base pair in one box. Follow its cross-lines to a target beyond the base band or stack.
Check the covers for each base digit across all three lines. If two cells act as one target, check the strong link that gives the group a single role.

copy.description: Trace the cross-lines from the bases to both target groups before checking the crossed-out candidates.
copy.reason: A base digit requires a copy on each cross-line. The cover count forces a copy into a target or a target group. Keep only candidates that fit the surviving assignments.

guide.start: Start with a base pair in one box. Follow its cross-lines to a target beyond the base band or stack.
guide.check: Check the covers for each base digit across all three lines. If two cells act as one target, check the strong link that gives the group a single role.
guide.reason: A base digit requires a copy on each cross-line. The cover count forces a copy into a target or a target group. Keep only candidates that fit the surviving assignments.

lessons.title: Double Exocet
lessons.summary: Compare two Exocets with shared cross-lines to rule out incompatible assignments.

paragraphs: Find two Exocet patterns that use the same cross-lines. Write down the possible base and target assignments for each.
Pair the assignments and check them together. Reject any pairing that repeats a digit in a house or makes the shared cross-lines impossible to fill.

copy.description: The grid marks cells from both components. Follow one complete pairing before deciding which candidates it supports.
copy.reason: Every solution must satisfy both Exocets at once. A target candidate can go if none of the compatible assignment pairs uses it.

guide.start: Find two Exocet patterns that use the same cross-lines. Write down the possible base and target assignments for each.
guide.check: Pair the assignments and check them together. Reject any pairing that repeats a digit in a house or makes the shared cross-lines impossible to fill.
guide.reason: Every solution must satisfy both Exocets at once. A target candidate can go if none of the compatible assignment pairs uses it.

groups.title: Advanced fish
groups.overview: Use boxes, overlapping houses, and chains to extend the basic fish rules.

lessons.title: Franken Fish
lessons.summary: Use at least one box as a base or cover in a single-digit fish.

paragraphs: Pick one digit and look for base houses whose candidate spots can be covered by the same number of houses. Include a box on one side.
Account for any candidate shared by two bases or left outside the covers. The proposed removal must account for every fin that could break the count.

copy.description: Read the highlighted bases and covers for digit 9. The box participates in the same count as the lines.
copy.reason: The base placements use the available cover spaces. A cover candidate can go when placing it would leave too little room for the bases, even after you account for fins.

guide.start: Pick one digit and look for base houses whose candidate spots can be covered by the same number of houses. Include a box on one side.
guide.check: Account for any candidate shared by two bases or left outside the covers. The proposed removal must account for every fin that could break the count.
guide.reason: The base placements use the available cover spaces. A cover candidate can go when placing it would leave too little room for the bases, even after you account for fins.

lessons.title: Mutant Fish
lessons.summary: Mix rows and columns on one side of a fish, then count how much room each candidate uses.

paragraphs: Choose one digit and look for a fish whose bases or covers mix rows and columns. Boxes can also take part.
Count how many bases and covers each candidate belongs to. Check uncovered and overlapping base spots before accepting a removal.

copy.description: The marked houses include a mixed set of lines. Follow the count for digit 4 through the overlaps.
copy.reason: If placing a candidate uses more cover spaces than it supplies base placements, the remaining bases can run out of room. Verify the result for every fin.

guide.start: Choose one digit and look for a fish whose bases or covers mix rows and columns. Boxes can also take part.
guide.check: Count how many bases and covers each candidate belongs to. Check uncovered and overlapping base spots before accepting a removal.
guide.reason: If placing a candidate uses more cover spaces than it supplies base placements, the remaining bases can run out of room. Verify the result for every fin.

lessons.title: Kraken Fish Type 1
lessons.summary: Use a fish’s normal removal and show that every possible fin also rules out the same candidate.

paragraphs: Look for a finned fish with a candidate the finless fish would remove. List all the fins that can break that fish.
For each fin, follow a chain from that fin being true. Every chain must rule out the same fish target.

copy.description: The crossed-out 2 is the fish target. Check its finless proof and each separate fin branch.
copy.reason: If all fins are false, the fish removes the candidate. If any fin is true, its chain removes the candidate. The removal holds in either case.

guide.start: Look for a finned fish with a candidate the finless fish would remove. List all the fins that can break that fish.
guide.check: For each fin, follow a chain from that fin being true. Every chain must rule out the same fish target.
guide.reason: If all fins are false, the fish removes the candidate. If any fin is true, its chain removes the candidate. The removal holds in either case.

references.label: HoDoKu on forcing proofs and Kraken Fish

lessons.title: Kraken Fish Type 2
lessons.summary: Start with a fish’s alternatives and follow chains to a shared removal anywhere on the grid.

paragraphs: Choose a line or cover involved in a finned fish. List the required fish-digit placements that remain possible, along with the fins that can break the fish.
Follow each listed placement through its chain. Look for a candidate that every branch rules out. It can be a different digit.

copy.description: Compare all branches leading to the crossed-out 7. This type can reach a target beyond the ordinary fish removal.
copy.reason: At least one fish or fin alternative must occur. If every alternative removes the same candidate, you can remove it from the current grid.

guide.start: Choose a line or cover involved in a finned fish. List the required fish-digit placements that remain possible, along with the fins that can break the fish.
guide.check: Follow each listed placement through its chain. Look for a candidate that every branch rules out. It can be a different digit.
guide.reason: At least one fish or fin alternative must occur. If every alternative removes the same candidate, you can remove it from the current grid.

references.label: HoDoKu on forcing proofs and Kraken Fish

groups.title: Pattern Overlay
groups.overview: Check full placements of one digit or several digits at a time.

lessons.title: Pattern Overlay
lessons.summary: Check every complete way to place one digit across the grid.

paragraphs: Pick one digit. Mark its placed copies and every empty cell where it is still a candidate.
Trace full layouts using one copy in each row, column, and box. Choose a row with few options to start.

copy.description: Try to build a complete layout for 4 that includes R2C5. The crossed-out 4 is absent from every valid layout.
copy.reason: A candidate can go if it appears in no full layout. If every full layout uses the same cell for the digit, you can place it there.

guide.start: Pick one digit. Mark its placed copies and every empty cell where it is still a candidate.
guide.check: Trace full layouts using one copy in each row, column, and box. Choose a row with few options to start.
guide.reason: A candidate can go if it appears in no full layout. If every full layout uses the same cell for the digit, you can place it there.

lessons.title: Two-digit Pattern Overlay
lessons.summary: Keep only full layouts for two digits that can fit together.

paragraphs: Pick two digits whose candidate layouts often use the same cells. Find the valid full layouts for each digit separately.
Pair the layouts and reject pairs that share a cell. Check whether each candidate is part of at least one surviving pair.

copy.description: Compare the layouts for 3 and 7. The crossed-out copies of 7 have layouts on their own, but none can share the grid with a 3 layout.
copy.reason: The two digits need separate cells. A layout that always collides with the other digit cannot occur, so any candidate supported only by those layouts can go.

guide.start: Pick two digits whose candidate layouts often use the same cells. Find the valid full layouts for each digit separately.
guide.check: Pair the layouts and reject pairs that share a cell. Check whether each candidate is part of at least one surviving pair.
guide.reason: The two digits need separate cells. A layout that always collides with the other digit cannot occur, so any candidate supported only by those layouts can go.

lessons.title: Three-digit Pattern Overlay
lessons.summary: Find candidates whose layouts can fit in pairs but fail when a third digit joins.

paragraphs: Pick three digits with few possible layouts. Start with the placements that already pass the two-digit checks.
Try to place one complete layout for each digit without sharing cells. Keep track of the candidates that appear in at least one valid triple.

copy.description: Check the highlighted digit layouts as a group. None of their compatible triples includes 4 in R9C2.
copy.reason: A layout for one digit can fit each other digit on its own and still fail to fit both at once. Only a three-way fit supports the candidate.

guide.start: Pick three digits with few possible layouts. Start with the placements that already pass the two-digit checks.
guide.check: Try to place one complete layout for each digit without sharing cells. Keep track of the candidates that appear in at least one valid triple.
guide.reason: A layout for one digit can fit each other digit on its own and still fail to fit both at once. Only a three-way fit supports the candidate.

lessons.title: Four-digit Pattern Overlay
lessons.summary: Check four digit layouts at once for a placement or removal missed by smaller groups.

paragraphs: Look for four digits whose few surviving layouts compete for the same cells. Reuse the results from their three-digit groups.
Try full layouts for all four digits together. Track any cell that the same digit uses in every surviving combination.

copy.description: All surviving combinations in the worked grid put 4 in R2C1. Check the four-layout fit before placing it.
copy.reason: Every valid solution contains a compatible set of four layouts. If all such sets put one digit in the same cell, that placement is forced.

guide.start: Look for four digits whose few surviving layouts compete for the same cells. Reuse the results from their three-digit groups.
guide.check: Try full layouts for all four digits together. Track any cell that the same digit uses in every surviving combination.
guide.reason: Every valid solution contains a compatible set of four layouts. If all such sets put one digit in the same cell, that placement is forced.

lessons.title: Five-digit Pattern Overlay
lessons.summary: Check a group of five digits for clashes that none of its four-digit groups can prove.
